title: Silk Road (Hornbill)
tagline: Nick Middleton’s drive across Tibet toward Mount Kailash: bleak roads, a departing driver and a chance meeting in Darchen.

overview.intro: A first-person travel account of the road from Ravu toward Mount Kailash, undertaken so that the narrator can walk the pilgrim circuit known as the kora. The journey proceeds by stages — the departure with his driver Tsetan, the crossing of the high Chang Tang, the grim settlement of Hor near Lake Manasarovar, and the arrival at Darchen, where illness and the absence of a companion leave him stuck until he meets Norbu. The unit studies how travel writing builds place through detail, how the narrative’s setbacks are paced, and how the account ends not with achievement but with the promise of one.

learn.title: The route: Ravu to the high plains

blocks.text: Travel writing depends on sequence, and Middleton structures his account as a series of legs, each with its own difficulty. He sets out from Ravu with his driver Tsetan, and the early miles establish the practical realities of the road: surfaces that deteriorate, altitudes that affect breathing, cold that gets into everything, and the long silences of the high plateau. The narrator’s voice is that of an academic who is candid about his own discomfort, which is the tonal signature of the piece — the humour comes from a scholar out of his depth rather than from any mockery of the country.

The landscape is presented through precise observation rather than through awe: the vast treeless plains, the changing light, animals encountered at distance, and the road itself as the story’s main character. That choice — to make the road the antagonist — is characteristic of the account, since nothing in it is dramatised; the difficulties are topographical and physical, and the prose earns its interest through accumulation of specific detail rather than through incident.

items: The account opens at Ravu, with Tsetan driving.
Each leg of the journey carries its own topographical difficulty.
The road itself, not a villain, is the antagonist.
The narrator’s candour about discomfort supplies the humour.
Place is built from precise observation rather than from awe.

learn.title: Hor: the anti-climax in the middle of the journey

blocks.text: The settlement of Hor is the account’s set-piece of disappointment. Approached through accounts that promised much, it proves to be bleak and dusty — a miserable contrast with the beauty earlier descriptions had led the reader to expect — and Middleton records its poverty, its wind and its insignificance without either romanticising or condemning it. The scene matters structurally as the low point of expectation: the reader has been primed for grandeur and is given a wretched village, and the gap between expectation and observation is the story’s most pointed piece of irony.

Hor also advances the journey’s argument about travel. Nothing on this route delivers what descriptions promised — the road is worse than maps suggest, the settlement worse than reports — and yet the account continues, because the point of the journey is not scenery but arrival at Kailash. The anti-climax therefore deepens rather than interrupts the narrative: it tests the narrator’s purpose and shows the reader that the goal is pilgrimage rather than tourism, even though the narrator himself would not use such language.

learn.title: Darchen, illness and the meeting with Norbu

blocks.text: At Darchen the journey stalls on two counts. The first is physical: the narrator has been unwell, and after weeks of altitude and cold he needs medical attention, which he seeks locally. The second is practical: the kora is a long circuit and walking it alone is neither wise nor, in his condition, possible, and the settlement offers no obvious companion. The account is honest about this low point — the adventurer is ill, bored and stuck — and that honesty is what keeps the piece from the genre of triumphalist travel writing.

Norbu’s arrival resolves the account without resolving the journey. He is a man with his own reasons for being there, and the two discover a shared intention to walk the circuit; the story ends with their decision to set out together rather than with any completion. The deferred ending is a deliberate craft choice: travel, the piece suggests, is composed of postponements and companionships rather than of conquests, and an account that ended at the summit would misrepresent how such journeys actually run. The reader closes on anticipation, which is where the narrator himself stood.

learn.title: How travel writing builds place and pace

blocks.text: The account’s two working instruments are specificity and pacing. Place is built from named, measured details — distances, altitudes, surfaces, temperatures, the look of a settlement at a given hour — rather than from adjectives of beauty, which gives the reader coordinates instead of impressions. Pace is controlled by the structure of legs: each movement ends with an arrival or a failure to arrive, so the narrative breathes at intervals without chapter marks, and the setbacks are distributed to keep deterioration gradual rather than melodramatic.

The narrator’s self-deprecation does real work too. By presenting himself as a geographer whose body is not equal to his curiosity, Middleton avoids two common failures of the genre: he does not pretend to mastery of the terrain, and he does not patronise the people along it. For extract answers, identify the type of detail quoted (measured, sensory, self-deprecating, ironic), say what place it builds, and place it within the journey’s sequence — travel writing answers reward knowing where in the route a passage sits.

questions.prompt: Describe the difficulties the narrator faces on the journey. Give four.
questions.answer: Four difficulties are: roads whose surfaces deteriorate, making progress slow and uncomfortable; the high, empty Chang Tang with thin air and punishing cold; the settlement of Hor, which proves bleak and dusty rather than the place descriptions had led him to expect; and illness on arrival at Darchen, combined with having no companion to walk the kora with, which stalls the entire purpose of the journey.
questions.explanation: Four distinct difficulties, at least two physical and one an anti-climax, are required.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the meeting with Norbu?
questions.answer: The meeting resolves the account’s human problem without resolving its central purpose: the narrator has been ill, alone and unable to set out on the kora, and Norbu arrives as a person with the same intention, so the two can walk together. Structurally it is the last event in a sequence of setbacks, and its timing converts the journey from a story about deprivation into one about chance companionship. It also justifies the deferred ending: the account closes on the decision to start rather than on arrival, which keeps faith with the way such journeys actually run — built from postponements and accidents of company rather than from conquest. Finally, it completes the narrator’s education in the trip: he set out as an individual traveller and ends by needing another person, which is the practical truth the road teaches.
questions.explanation: Four functions are required: practical resolution, structural reversal, justification of the open ending, and the narrator’s changed understanding.

questions.prompt: How does Middleton build the place he travels through? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: Middleton builds place through accumulated specificity rather than through impression, and the method is consistent across the account. Distances, altitudes, surfaces and temperatures are named, so the reader receives coordinates rather than scenery: the road out of Ravu deteriorates in measurable stages, the Chang Tang is defined by its emptiness and cold, and Darchen is presented through its practical offerings — medical attention, shelter, the absence of suitable company — rather than through its appearance. Second, place is built by expectation against observation: earlier descriptions and accounts promise much, and Hor is then given as bleak and dusty, so the settlement is characterised partly by the gap between report and reality — a technique that describes the place and simultaneously comments on the sources that describe places. Third, the narrator’s own condition serves as an instrument: his illness, breathlessness and boredom register the altitude and climate in the body rather than on the page, which lets the reader feel the place instead of only seeing it. Fourth, people enter the account only as functions of the road — the driver who knows its surfaces, the stranger who shares the destination — so that the landscape remains the true subject and each human figure measures it. The leg-by-leg structure supports all of this by giving each location a stage in the sequence, so the reader holds a route rather than a gallery. Answers should quote two measured details and one moment of disappointed expectation, and locate them in the journey’s order, because travel writing is judged on whether the examiner can reconstruct the route from the answer.
questions.explanation: Full marks require at least three techniques with quotations from different stages of the journey and an account of how the sequence organises the place.

questions.prompt: Is the account a record of a journey, or an argument about travelling itself? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case for record is supported by the account’s evident fidelity to sequence and circumstance. The route is given stage by stage — departure from Ravu, the crossing of the high plains, Hor, Darchen — and within each stage the details are practical rather than reflective: surfaces, distances, weather, illness, money, company. The narrator observes rather than interprets, his humour arises from circumstance rather than from design, and the two human figures who matter, Tsetan and Norbu, appear as parts of the journey’s logistics rather than as characters in a thesis. Read this way the piece belongs squarely to the documentary travelogue, where the achievement is attention rather than argument. The case for an argument about travelling rests on how deliberately the account frustrates the genre’s conventions. Every expectation is set up to be disappointed — the road worse than mapped, Hor bleaker than described, Darchen reached only to be stalled by illness and solitude — and the cumulative effect of these disappointments is a claim: travel is not the sequence of grandeur that travel writing itself advertises. The narrator’s candour about his own weakness supports the claim, because he presents himself as a man whose curiosity exceeds his fitness, which is the ordinary condition of travellers rather than the heroic one the genre prefers. The ending is the strongest evidence of all: the account stops at the point of departure rather than achievement, resolving in companionship — the chance arrival of Norbu — instead of conquest of the circuit, and a text that meant only to record a journey could have ended at any point of completion. The balanced judgement is that the record is the argument’s evidence: Middleton arranges real detail so that its pattern makes the case, and the distinction between reporting and claiming collapses when every reported disappointment points the same way. Answers should therefore cite two documentary details and two frustrated expectations, and conclude about how selection rather than commentary carries the argument, because this account never states its thesis — it demonstrates it stage by stage.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings with evidence from different parts of the account, the observation that the ending refuses the conventional triumph, and a judgement about how selection produces argument without statement.
